chapters.title: Chapter 1: NOI and Cap Rate Fundamentals

lessons.title: What Cap Rate Really Measures: The Unlevered Return on a Property

children.text: Vikram, a chartered accountant in Bengaluru, is looking at a 5,000 sq ft Grade-A office unit on Outer Ring Road for ₹4.5 crore. The broker's pitch has one number underlined twice: "This is an 8% cap rate deal, sir. Very good for this market." Vikram has heard the term before, on REIT investor calls and in CBRE reports, but he has never actually built the number himself. Before he wires any money, he wants to know exactly what that 8% is measuring, and just as importantly, what it is not measuring. By the end of this lesson you will be able to calculate cap rate from scratch, and know precisely what question it answers.

body.text: Cap rate answers exactly one question: if you paid the full price in cash today, with no loan at all, what percentage of that price would the property hand back to you in net income this year? It says nothing about your loan, your tax bill, or what the property might sell for later.

children.text: The Cap Rate Formula

markDefs.definition: Capitalization rate: net operating income divided by purchase price, expressed as a percentage. The standard first-pass measure of an income property's return, independent of financing.
Net Operating Income: the rental income a property generates in a year, after operating expenses like property tax, insurance, maintenance and vacancy, but before loan payments and income tax.

children.text: The
capitalization rate
, or cap rate, is the property's
net operating income

divided by its purchase price. NOI is what is left of rental income once you subtract the operating costs needed to run the property, but before you subtract a single rupee of loan interest or principal. Building NOI properly, line by line, is the entire subject of the next lesson. For now, take it as given.

body.caption: Both NOI and purchase price are measured in the same currency, so the cap rate is a pure percentage, comparable across a ₹50 lakh flat and a ₹500 crore mall.

children.text: Vikram gets the rent roll and expense statement from the seller. Gross annual rent on the ORR unit is ₹40,80,000. After property tax, common area maintenance not recovered from the tenant, insurance and a small vacancy allowance, NOI works out to ₹36,00,000. On a ₹4,50,00,000 purchase price, that is: ₹36,00,000 ÷ ₹4,50,00,000 × 100 = 8.0%. The broker's number checks out, at least on the surface.

body.text: A cap rate is only as honest as the NOI behind it. A broker who starts from gross rent instead of NOI, or who quietly drops the vacancy allowance, can turn a genuine 6.5% deal into an advertised 8%. Always ask for the actual rent agreement and expense statement, not a one-line summary.

children.text: Why "Unlevered" Is the Whole Point

markDefs.definition: A return calculated as if the entire purchase were paid in cash, with no loan involved. Cap rate is always an unlevered, going-in return.

children.text: Cap rate is deliberately an
unlevered

measure. It uses the full purchase price as its base, not your down payment, and it never touches loan interest. That is a feature, not a gap. It means Vikram's 8.0% and a cash buyer's 8.0% on the identical unit are the same number, even if Vikram funds 70% of the price with a loan from HDFC Bank and the other buyer pays entirely in cash. Cap rate describes the asset. It has nothing to say about how any particular buyer chose to pay for it.

children.text: Cap Rate and Price Move in Opposite Directions

Two floors in the same ORR building are on the market. Both are identical 5,000 sq ft units leased to the same kind of IT-services tenant at the same rent, so both throw off an NOI of ₹36,00,000. Unit A is priced at ₹4.5 crore, the one Vikram is evaluating. Unit B, on a higher floor with a better view, is priced at ₹5 crore for the same income.

body.caption: Same NOI, different price, different cap rate

children.text: Unit B's cap rate is lower even though the income is identical, simply because the buyer is paying more for the same rupee of NOI. This is the same relationship a Nifty investor already knows from the equity market: a stock with a higher P/E ratio is paying more per rupee of earnings, which usually means the market expects either lower risk or faster growth ahead. A lower cap rate means the market is paying a premium for that asset's income. A higher cap rate means the market is demanding a discount, usually because it sees more risk in that income continuing.

body.title: Reading the relationship
body.question: Two identical warehouses near Bhiwandi, Maharashtra earn the same NOI of ₹60,00,000 a year. Warehouse P is priced at ₹6.67 crore, giving a 9.0% cap rate. Warehouse Q is priced at ₹8.57 crore. What is Warehouse Q's cap rate, and what does the difference imply?
options: About 7.0%, implying the market sees Warehouse Q as lower risk or higher growth
About 11.0%, implying the market sees Warehouse Q as lower risk or higher growth
About 9.0%, cap rate is unaffected by price
It cannot be calculated without the loan amount
body.explanation: ₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹8,57,00,000 × 100 ≈ 7.0%. Warehouse Q's buyer is paying more for the identical income stream, so the cap rate is lower. That premium usually reflects something the market likes better about Q: a stronger tenant, a longer lease, a better location, or simply lower perceived risk.

children.text: What Typical Cap Rates Look Like Across Indian Real Estate

Brokerages such as CBRE, JLL and Knight Frank, and listed REITs like Embassy Office Parks, Mindspace Business Parks and Brookfield India, publish cap rate benchmarks every quarter. The ranges below are illustrative and move with interest rates and demand, so treat them as a rough map of where different asset classes sit relative to each other, not as today's live number.

body.text: Residential sits far below every commercial category here, echoing the yield compression you have already seen in this track. Buyers accept a much lower running yield on a home partly because they are pricing in appreciation, and partly because owning a home is rarely a purely financial decision the way a warehouse or an office floor is.

body.title: Calculate a cap rate
body.prompt: A small commercial unit in BKC, Mumbai is priced at ₹6,00,00,000. Its NOI, after all operating expenses, is ₹42,00,000 a year. What is its cap rate? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹42,00,000 ÷ ₹6,00,00,000 × 100 = 7.0%. Sitting at the lower end of the Grade-A office range, this would be read as a premium-priced, lower-risk asset relative to Vikram's 8.0% ORR unit, everything else being equal.

children.text: What Cap Rate Does Not Tell You
Cap rate is a single-year, unlevered snapshot, and it is easy to ask more of it than it can give. It says nothing about three things you will need before you actually buy:
How financing changes your actual return.
Once Vikram takes a loan, his return on the cash he actually puts in can be higher or lower than 8.0%. That is cash-on-cash return, covered from Chapter 2.
What the property might sell for later.
Cap rate says nothing about appreciation or the exit price. A property can have a healthy cap rate today and still be a poor investment if the exit cap rate expands. Chapter 4 covers this.
How reliable that NOI really is.

An 8.0% cap rate resting on a single tenant whose lease expires next year is not the same quality of 8.0% as one resting on a diversified rent roll with long leases. Chapter 3 covers the red flags to check for.

body.title: The defining feature of cap rate
body.textWithBlank: Cap rate is calculated using the full purchase price, which is why it is described as an ___ return: it ignores how the buyer actually financed the purchase.
body.explanation: Cap rate treats every buyer as if they paid entirely in cash. That is what makes it useful for comparing very different properties on one scale, and it is also exactly what it leaves out.

cards.definition: NOI divided by purchase price, expressed as a percentage. An unlevered, single-year return on a property.
Net Operating Income: rental income after operating expenses, before loan payments and tax.
A return calculated as if the property were bought entirely in cash, with no loan.
The cap rate calculated at the time of purchase, using the first year's expected NOI.
For a fixed NOI, a higher purchase price means a lower cap rate, and vice versa.

points: Cap rate = NOI ÷ Purchase Price × 100, an unlevered, all-cash, single-year return on a property.
It ignores financing on purpose, which is what lets you compare a ₹50 lakh flat and a ₹500 crore mall on the same footing.
For a fixed NOI, price and cap rate move in opposite directions: paying more for the same income means a lower cap rate.
A lower cap rate usually signals the market sees lower risk or higher growth potential in that income; a higher cap rate usually prices in more risk.
Indian Grade-A office typically trades around 7.0%-8.5%, warehousing and retail higher, residential rental far lower, but always verify current figures before underwriting a real deal.
Cap rate says nothing about your financing, your exit price, or how reliable the underlying NOI actually is. Those are the next three chapters.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, prices and cap rates are illustrative. Real estate cap rates, interest rates and market conditions change, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser or a chartered accountant before making any decision.
